papers.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
papers.abstract: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness. The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.

papers.title: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and the potential for cross-provider adaptability. Achieved without memory, evolution, or extensions, these results establish EvoX as a competitive multi-model agent runtime and underscore the importance of harness-level operational control in realizing foundation-model capabilities.

papers.title: Auditable Authorization for LLM Agents: Empirical Evidence Across Model, Harness, and Workflow Layers
papers.abstract: Human approval provides effective control only if rejected work stops and authorized work completes. We formalize refusal safety and bounded authorization completeness, and audit three execution boundaries: the model selects a call, the harness schedules and resumes it, and the workflow routes the decision to a protected effect. Paired decisions, exact traces, and native business-state witnesses support experiments with three models, five prompt arms, four runtime approval designs, two additional framework replays, and 100 public workflow sources. The paired model panel leaves seven of 300 approvals unfinished despite zero denied effects; parallel confirmation loses an approved branch in three tasks per model, restoration omits 336/672 CrewAI approvals, and four of 59 comparable n8n workflows execute after Reject. Comparing intent, generated calls, dispatch, and native effects identifies the first observable divergence and its repair target. This yields a practical audit contract that makes both refusal safety and authorization completeness independently verifiable, converting human approval from a procedural formality into an enforceable control boundary between intent and real-world effect.

papers.title: When Facts Change, Which Decisions Break? Dependency-Aware Context Graphs for Agents
papers.abstract: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. We investigate the reliability-cost trade-off of field-level dependency graphs extracted from actual agent read traces. A controlled benchmark spans three executable workflow domains and four successive updates, with independent imperative and expression-based references. Across 120 workflows, two models and two repeated runs, we compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies and verified dependency upper bounds. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. The results distinguish potential dependency impact from actual decision invalidity and show why selective repair must be evaluated with both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost. The evidence concerns explicit procedural workflows; broad real-world agent-memory generalization remains untested.

papers.title: Beyond Prompts: Runtime Contracts for Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents act on repositories through shell commands and file edits, and teams steer them with written engineering rules. Industrial settings expect such rules to be enforced and their application to be evidenced, and a rule given as prompt text provides neither. We test whether executable contracts enforced while the agent works reduce rule violations compared with the same rules in the prompt, retrieved as guidance, or checked only after generation. Violations are scored by an oracle whose methods differ from the in-loop checks, and the oracle is validated by two human reviewers and a model reviewer. Across three studies on two model families (240, 112 and 108 runs), enforcement during execution produced no oracle-detected violation in 104 paired runs, against 21 to 55% of runs without rules, and no loss of functional correctness in the two confirmatory studies. In the confirmatory study on tasks aimed at known failure situations (Study 3, protocol hashed before the first run), enforcement lowered the share of violating runs by 31 percentage points relative to no rules (Holm-adjusted p = 0.014); the 17-point difference from prompted rules was not significant (p = 0.12), and neither was any contrast in Study 2, where only 3 of 14 tasks produced a violation. Prompted rules removed some violation types but not recursive deletes of scratch directories, and checks after generation repaired file edits but not commands that had already run. That enforcement satisfies the rules it enforces is expected by construction; what the data add is where prompting falls short, the absence of a functional cost, and the limits of the rules and of the oracle themselves. The studies use low-cost models and one small fixture.

papers.title: SwarmSafe-Delta: Isolating Message Effects on LLM Agent Safety
papers.abstract: When a tool-using LLM agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether an upstream message changed the executor's action. We introduce SwarmSafe-Delta, a paired executable protocol that freezes upstream computation, varies real, hidden, and format-matched placebo delivery, and scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets. Across four models and constructed optional tasks, real delivery at $N=4$ produces 21.4% risky-world violations, versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 percentage points). Real delivery also improves benign task success, illustrating that suppressing communication sacrifices utility. In a second regime constructed to require an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. These effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates. Exploratory action-level analyses show that the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution; model differences also largely track these message compositions. The contribution is a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol rather than a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.

papers.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. A state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates enforce these assets during execution; an independent auditor grades the resulting trace. The assets are updated only after a regression check and human approval .We evaluate the method on three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps. On Domain A, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation set shows unattended completion rising from 50% to 100%, retrieval recall from 56% to 91.67%, and end-to-end latency dropping from 440 to 159 minutes, with scenario-analysis recall rising from 45% to 93%. Two other domains were taken over by teams that did not write the assets, one in four days and one in seven days. A controlled ablation separates the two failure sources. The code is available at https://github.com/ZTE-AICloud/Co-Sight/tree/master/Co-Sight%20Harness.

papers.title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

papers.title: System Optimizations for Cost-Efficient Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: AI agent harnesses play the critical role of providing LLMs with an interface to a computing environment. Recent studies show that AI agents' task-execution accuracy depends mostly on the LLM used, while harness-side variances such as system prompts or tools have minimal impact. Rather, such harness-side variances show a larger impact on the cost of agent executions, achieving cost reductions up to 2.6 times on the same model and task. To further explore these harness-side cost optimization opportunities, we analyze the cost accumulation patterns across various agent traces and identify system opportunities to reduce token use and LLM calls without modifying the model or affecting task accuracy. Based on this analysis, we design Agency, a harness interposition platform that provides a unified abstraction and allows easy and portable implementation of harness-side system optimizations on existing off-the-shelf harnesses such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex. Using Agency, we implement proof-of-concept optimization techniques based on our analysis and achieve cost reductions up to 35% across various real-world benchmarks on existing harnesses without compromising accuracy.

papers.title: Logical AI OS: A Training-Free Governance Layer Outside the Model for Instruction Following -- Benefits, Costs, Failures, and the Calibration of the Measuring Instrument Itself
papers.abstract: Small language models often fail explicit user requests (length, number of items, format, required or forbidden words, grammatical person, answer language). We measure a training-free governance layer placed outside the model: it reads the requests with rules, checks the answer mechanically, repairs it when a request is not kept, and hands back the original answer when the repair fails. The loop exists in prior work; our contribution is measuring its benefits, costs and failures, and reporting how the measuring instrument itself was calibrated. On four 4-bit Qwen-family models (3B, 7B, 14B, one 7B reasoning model) and 329 Chinese prompts: (1) answers that keep every request the layer read rise significantly (all comparisons p<0.0001), by 34 to 66 of 329 under the corrected checker and 52 to 92 after a length-control fix; a generic redo message brings no significant gain. (2) Exploratory: on 90 repair-triggered prompts, two AI annotators found the layer produced an acceptable answer where the bare model did not more often than the reverse (49:7; 18:12, not significant). (3) Costs: 43-66% more generation time; whole-answer rewriting makes a sizeable share of usable answers unusable. (4) Failures: rule-based reading reaches about 70% and 84% of a two-annotator ceiling on unseen phrasings; unsatisfiable requests make the reasoning model loop; model self-reports are unreliable (18 of 25 "fixed" items were not fixed). (5) Over half of the original checker's "violated" verdicts on structural requests were wrong; after correction the main result holds, and one comparison is downgraded. Conclusions are limited to this Chinese material, the Qwen family and sizes up to 14B. The governance implementation is not released; data, answers, verdicts and the checker are public.

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent
papers.abstract: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34x the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [-5.3, +7.2]). Judged against the measured run-to-run noise, under a rule written before the test was opened, the first is a real saving and the second is not. This is a case study of one agent and nine test questions, not a general result.

papers.title: MemCredit: From Relevance to Utility for Decision-Time Memory in Long-Horizon Web Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. We introduce MemCredit, a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility. MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

papers.title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured. To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations. Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

papers.title: One Run Is Not Enough: Reminding a small Gemma 4 coding agent of its last finding made no measurable difference in a paired test
papers.abstract: When a coding agent runs out of room, its earlier findings are cut and it forgets them. We tested a simple fix: automatically putting the agent's last finding back in front of it. We fixed the rules in advance and ran 98 paired coding tasks with and without this reminder, using Gemma 4 31B (QAT, 4-bit) in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent harness. The reminder made no measurable difference: across all 98 tasks, 47 were solved with it and 48 without (-1.0 points, 95% interval [-8.3, +6.3], exact McNemar p=1.0). The primary outcome (a documented deviation from our preregistration), the first 48 pairs, was 29/48 with memory against 25/48 without (+8.3 points, [-2.1, +18.3], p=0.22); the extension of 50 tasks, decided after that result, pointed the other way (18/50 against 23/50, -10.0 points, p=0.125), so the sign did not replicate. With 19% of tasks flipping between two identical no-memory runs, the combined interval excludes harms larger than about 8 points and gains larger than about 6, and the design had 80% power only for effects of about +-12 points or more. The model almost never wrote notes (2 of 16 and 4 of 32 runs), and memory cost context: the first request is larger and something was injected at only 47% to 65% of compactions. The registered secondary, repeated actions per compaction, was also null. Two directional hypotheses found on Modal did not replicate on Kaggle. We also report an A/A calibration and a validity funnel (129 tasks, 105 valid). Together these results show that single-run memory claims on task sets of this size sit inside run-to-run noise. The treatment is a harness mechanism and does not test agent-written memory.

papers.title: Anatomy of an Agent Harness: Decisions, Invariants and Corner Cases
papers.abstract: An agent harness is the program around a language model that turns its replies into actions: it builds each request, runs the tools the model asks for, decides what the model may do without asking, stores the conversation, recovers from failures, and shows a person what happened. Most of these decisions are made in code and rarely written down, so each harness meets the same corner cases again. This paper writes them down as invariants to test. It gives a system model with trust boundaries; 30 decision cards in six groups, each with options and costs, an invariant, the corner cases that break it, a test and an evidence tag; six cause classes for failures; a test method built on scripted providers, recorded behaviour and planted changes; and a checklist. The cards come from building one desktop harness, Crewroom, the author's own, and from manually testing ten other harnesses and studying open-source harnesses as reference; some patterns in the cards were adopted from those, so the catalogue is not independent of them. Of the 83 invariant clauses, 56 are tagged Tested, 12 Believed and 15 Open. The checklist is applied to the author's harness as one worked example, by its builder with no second rater: of its 30 items, 11 hold, 14 do not and 5 were not tested. It is not a ranking. The paper makes no claims about answer quality or cost or other platforms, and does not evaluate or rank other harnesses.

papers.title: Reconfigurable Action Theories: A Formal Foundation for Dynamically Composable Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Action theories typically fix their vocabulary and causal laws, whereas agent harnesses can change their tools, providers, and policies during execution. We introduce Reconfigurable Action Theories (RAT), in which actions can change the action theory itself. A theory module in RAT contains a vocabulary, causal laws, and an initializer. A RAT configuration records the active modules and the world state. Module loading and unloading are represented by actions governed by ordinary causal laws. RAT retains the standard causal action semantics of its language fragment when the active module set is fixed. We give sufficient conditions for at most one next configuration, preservation of existing behavior when a module is added, and equal results when modules are loaded in either order. We establish the computational complexity of reasoning tasks in RAT and translate finite RAT systems into nonmonotonic causal theories and Answer Set Programming (ASP), preserving bounded executions. Experiments compare finite RAT models with executions of official DeepSeek Harness, Pi, and OpenHands implementations. RAT provides a formal basis for checking how component changes affect a harness's available actions, behavior, and reachable goals.

papers.title: Recovery Gone Too Far: Understanding and Repairing Risky Fallback in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through tools, reading repositories, running builds, and pushing code. When a tool fails with an ordinary error, such as a rate limit or a timeout, the agent can fall back to a substitute tool and still complete the task. However, the same fallback that completes a task in one environment can cross an action boundary in another. For example, after a push is rejected, a forced push in one repository replaces only the agent's own commits, while in a different repository it also removes another author's commits. We call such a fallback a risky fallback. To understand this phenomenon, we conduct an empirical study on 304 scenarios that span eight domains and cover 55 real CVEs. All four mainstream models we evaluate exhibit risky fallback, with action-boundary violations in up to 96.8% of risky scenarios. We further evaluate three mainstream mitigations and find that none of them is effective against risky fallback. We then present nrepair. At each call to the substitute tool, nrepair scores the agent's context with a monitor whose threshold is calibrated on normal runs alone; when the monitor triggers, it withholds the call once and returns the decision to the agent. nrepair reduces action-boundary violations on all four models, by up to 76.0% (from 67.5% to 16.2%), at a negligible runtime cost. On most models, the normal success rate drops by less than 7%. We also evaluate nrepair on two production agents, Claude Code and Codex, and find that it is equally effective on both.

papers.title: Calibrating Document-Local Boundaries for Contextual Chunk Retrieval
papers.abstract: Late Chunking encodes an entire document before pooling at chunk boundaries, preserving document context in local retrieval units. Chunk-level post-training improves context-dependent retrieval, but shared context can make semantically similar same-document negatives difficult to distinguish. We study the local decision boundary between a gold chunk and its hardest sibling. Starting from InSeNT, we analyze InSeNT's within-document gradients and show that the entropy of the conditional negative allocation decreases monotonically with the scaling factor at fixed logits. We propose a two-part framework for calibrating document-local chunk boundaries. The first component adapts the discriminative scale from within-document margins, while the second exposes chunk partitions to attention during document encoding. Experiments on ConTEB and NanoBEIR show that the resulting model improves contextual chunk retrieval across the evaluated encoder settings while retaining competitive passage-level retrieval quality; ablations further characterize the distinct roles of adaptive scaling and chunk-aware routing.

papers.title: DISCERN: Preserve at Write, Resolve at Read for Persistent LLM-Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents accumulate memory across dozens of sessions in which facts contradict, get superseded, and blur as similarly named entities collide in embedding space. The field treats this as a retrieval problem; we show it is not. On ENT-310, a synthetic enterprise sales-agent memory benchmark of 310 queries (210 answerable, 100 unanswerable), a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reader over a memory store already matches strong memory systems on the recall pillars. Retention and currency are near-saturated, roughly 0.93 to 0.98 for every competent system, so recall is essentially solved. What remains unsolved is resolution: which entity a query refers to, which time-state is current, and whether to commit an answer at all or decline when evidence is insufficient. We propose DISCERN (DISambiguation and Cross-session Episodic memoRy Navigation), an agent-memory framework built on a single rule: preserve at write, resolve at read. At write time DISCERN builds a strictly additive bi-temporal provenance graph that never merges confusable entities and never drops superseded values. At read time a zero-LLM tool surface drives an agentic loop that navigates this graph and commits exactly one of four gated terminal actions. A four-judge LLM-as-a-Judge council scores two axes: answer correctness on answerable questions, and the answer-versus-abstain decision as a classification problem. On ENT-310, DISCERN is the best-calibrated system on abstention (F1 0.924 versus at most 0.802 across eight baselines) and leads macro answer correctness under equal pillar weighting (0.861 versus 0.806 for the strongest baseline), a lead driven by entity resolution (0.800, where no baseline exceeds 0.40). Applied with zero tuning to the full LoCoMo corpus, the same pipeline again leads macro answer correctness (0.663 versus 0.638) and stays among the best-calibrated on false-premise abstention.

papers.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
papers.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

papers.title: Dependable Long-Horizon LLM Agents: A Trajectory-Centered Empirical Study of Where Errors Enter and Which Controls Reach Them
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent fails part-way through a long task, the usual analysis records a symptom: a failure-mode label, or the agent and step judged responsible. It does not say where the error entered, which state carried it to the symptom, whether anything in the trajectory contradicted it, or which control could have caught it. We define an episode record that ties a candidate fault to its origin, propagation, detection, response and consequence, located by operational phase and state domain, and that names the control families whose observation and reach cover it. We turned the record into a written annotation protocol and applied it to 95 failed runs of six multi-agent systems from the public Who&When and MAD corpora, reading each trajectory in full. Faults enter early (median at 0.18 of the run), mostly as wrong decisions or fabrications over task state, and in 37 of 88 Who&When runs before the step the corpus' human labels mark as decisive. In 72% of failed runs the trajectory already contained evidence against the error before the failure; in 88% of those no agent acted on it. Something flagged a deviation in 31% of runs, but no response removed the deviated state. Independent judges reading the unused evidence, task contracts fixed at admission, and re-checking beliefs against the environment reach most episodes; restoring the agent's own state would have sufficed in 35 of 95 runs. A text scan of the raw corpus also shows that 45% of the hand-crafted Who&When failures ended with a provider content-filter crash after which the harness emitted a final answer no agent produced, a failure class that neither symptom taxonomies nor responsible-agent labels represent. Protocol, records and scripts are included.

papers.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

papers.title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
papers.abstract: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.

papers.title: Correct First, Fast Second: What a Local 7B Code Model Can and Cannot Do for GPU Kernel Optimization
papers.abstract: We study how much the interaction strategy around a fixed, locally hosted 7B-parameter code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) affects its ability to replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels. On 30 KernelBench tasks (levels 1-3, first 10 each, evaluated on a V100), we compare four regimes of increasing structure: zero-shot prompting, profiling-guided prompting, iterative refinement on execution feedback, and a multi-agent loop (analysis, retrieval, generation, evaluation, feedback triage) in which the same model fills four roles around a non-LLM evaluator. Three findings stand out. (1) Correctness, not speed, is the binding constraint: even correct generated kernels average 0.97-0.99x the speed of eager PyTorch, because a 7B model cannot out-write cuBLAS/cuDNN on dense GEMM and convolution; the only real wins are fused memory-bound epilogues. (2) The best strategy depends on difficulty: profiling-guided prompting is strongest overall (43% correct, 27% faster than baseline), but the agent loop is the only method that solves any level-2 fusion problem (3/10 vs. 0/10 for all others). (3) Naive agentic scaffolding is actively harmful: our first agent scored 3% correct, below zero-shot's 30%, and the decisive repairs were matching the agent's ambition to the model's competence and spending compute on best-of-n sampling under a real execution oracle (3% to 33% correct from n=1 to n=8), not on more reasoning steps.

papers.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
papers.abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. It combines (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, (2) a 2D product taint lattice $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trust}} \times \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sens}}$ and a workspace provenance ledger that prevents secret laundering across disk, (3) deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and (4) bytecode certificates, split-horizon audit logs, self-healing security test synthesis, and an adaptive UserWikiManager. Across $N=252$ fixtures ($120$ attack, $120$ benign, $12$ kill chains), a live local LLM judge (qwen3:4b) refuses $98.3\%$ of benign work at $142.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ latency, whereas Ring 0 achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ in $12.7\,μ\mathrm{s}$ ($11{,}200\times$ faster). In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy misses $4/12$ kill chains ($\mathrm{ABR}=0.667$) and coarse Boolean taint blocks $83.3\%$ of benign workflows, while our 2D product lattice achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ at $\approx 20\,μ\mathrm{s}$ per step.

papers.title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing
papers.abstract: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

papers.title: Contain, Conform, Compare (Extended Version): A Red-Teamed Evaluation Kit for Small Coding Agents and the Full Record of Its Experiments
papers.abstract: A hosted score in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent competition is one noisy number, so development needs a local evaluator that is fast, safe for agent-written code, and matching the hosted scorer's prompts. drydock-eval evaluates a small coding agent (Gemma 4 E4B) at about 250 runs per hour on one RTX 5090. Contain runs each job in a fresh container without network and passed 200 scripted escape tests; conform provides eight checks that compare a local stack's requests with the scorer's configuration, down to rendered tokens; compare provides paired statistics that respect repository clusters. AI agents built and attacked the kit; a human owner approved machine use and release. This extended version repeats the short paper and adds the full record of the experiments made with and around the kit: 9,660 rows of agent runs, 2,494 grading controls and 72 serving measurements, all released. On four L4 GPUs the 31B model decodes 38.1 tokens per second in one stream and E4B 105.8. Six configurations of a 31B agent solved between 37 and 44 of 70 development tasks, and no pairwise difference was detected. A pre-registered five-arm experiment (231 tasks, 4,620 jobs) measured four prompt divergences: no E4B solve-rate change was detected (largest estimate -2.1 points, 95% interval -4.4 to +0.4). Three changes of the E4B agent led their screens by +1.0 to +6.2 points; each was then tested once on new tasks under a frozen pass rule, and none was confirmed (gains -0.35, -0.39 and +4.10 points). The unchanged baseline, run again on the same 128 tasks, moved by 1.17 points, and 65% of these tasks were solved in none of eight runs. Prompts and agent bundles are withheld; every run-level result is public.

papers.title: StaleBench: Isolating Stale Retrieval in Agent Memory, and Pricing the Fix
papers.abstract: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.

papers.title: Lost in Delegation: Studying the Effectiveness of Task Orchestration in Generative Search
papers.abstract: LLMs have quickly evolved from models used in isolation to agentic systems that delegate tasks to external tools and other LLMs to solve complex assignments. This agentic augmentation has led to impressive capability gains. However, when and how delegation improves performance remains poorly understood. For example, it is unclear whether delegation helps when tasks involve post-cutoff information that the orchestrating LLM cannot reliably resolve from its own knowledge. In this work, we use purpose-built datasets with pre- and post-cutoff splits to compare various delegation modes. We find that delegation provides no consistent accuracy improvement over non-delegated setups, with effects varying across models and tasks. When tasks involve knowledge unavailable to the orchestrator, delegation can substantially degrade accuracy, while direct tool use with the same LLM performs much better. Our analysis identifies distorted delegated queries, inefficient tool use, and failures to preserve and use information between agents as recurring failure modes. These findings suggest that effective orchestration requires both well-calibrated delegation decisions and effective exchange of information between agents.

papers.title: ParseBench-2: Severity-Aware Evaluation of Document Parsing
papers.abstract: Document-parsing metrics can give high scores to outputs that change important facts and penalize changes that preserve meaning. People can often judge these consequences more easily than they can design a metric to measure them. We introduce a method for developing parsing metrics from severity policies that specify how each error type should affect the score. We express these policies through test scenarios that specify how a metric should behave. We then optimize the metric implementations against these fixed expectations, using coding agents to refine comparison rules, error detectors and weights under human review. This makes stated human priorities an explicit objective of metric design. We apply this method in ParseBench-2, a comprehensive document-parsing benchmark that combines broad capability coverage with metrics calibrated to error severity. It covers 4,317 pages across six dimensions of parsing quality: text, formatting, tables, charts, visual grounding, and forms. We use detailed annotations and targeted difficult cases to check for changed facts, broken structural relationships, and missing content. We take the lower of a parsing score that measures content recovery and a severity cap that penalizes detected errors, so recovering most of a page cannot hide a serious error. Across six severity test suites, our metrics more closely match the expert judgments expressed by the scenario targets than existing metrics and penalize at most 3.4% of the tested benign variations. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation spanning frontier vision-language models, specialized document parsers and open-weight systems, comparing their overall rankings, performance across parsing capabilities and tradeoffs between accuracy and cost.

papers.title: Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories: A Controlled Study of Agent Memory Evaluation
papers.abstract: An answer can match the reference for a complete agent history even when the reader's visible history does not determine it. We study this distinction using executable device logs. Our protocol separates reference agreement, certified evidence sufficiency, and context-appropriate behavior. Insufficiency requires two legal histories yielding byte-identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology and query cutoffs certify sufficient prefixes. On 80 confirmation histories, Qwen3-32B matches 87 hidden references among 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, with only seven appropriate abstentions. A fixed-input DeepSeek-V4-Flash replication matches 85 and abstains on 21 of the same 203 instances. Each reader makes 1,600 requests. Compact CSV's estimated appropriateness effects remain inconclusive: +3.16 percentage points, clustered 95% interval [0.00,6.57], for Qwen and +2.46, [-1.84,6.94], for DeepSeek. A separate held-out judge study achieves 99.38% correctness but retains support errors and truncations; a deterministic baseline solves all constructed cases. These results support an evaluation diagnosis across two hosted reader configurations, not gains for a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.

papers.title: Beyond Clumsy Agentic Tool Calling: How Cueing and Spotting Make the Difference
papers.abstract: LLM-based task-oriented agents depend on tools to interact with their environments, but may overlook execution feedback, repeat ineffective calls, or persist with unproductive strategies. These behaviors can hinder agents' ability to use tools autonomously and sustain task progress. We characterize tool-use symptoms at two temporal granularities: local clumsy tool-use behaviors and tool-use detours spanning multiple interactions. Towards greater autonomy in tool use, we present ToolPulse, an online middleware supporting autonomous tool use through cueing and spotting. ToolPulse tracks execution state and temporal interaction patterns, monitoring proposed calls before dispatch and inspecting execution feedback prior to the agent resumes reasoning. It combines state-based rules, semantic sequence analysis, and interaction-feature similarity to identify intervention opportunities and provide verbal reminders, structured feedback, or context-specific advice from auxiliary models. Our process-oriented evaluation distinguishes trigger validity, behavioral cessation, and substantive correction alongside task outcomes and resource costs. Using SWE-agent with three backbone models, we evaluate 1,350 trajectories on 90 Python, C++, and Java bug-fix tasks, comparing unassisted execution with four assistance strategies. Substantive responses follow 61.6-90.9% of valid triggers for tool-use detours. Concise reminders achieve the highest observed aggregate substantive-response rate; more elaborate assistance offers symptom-dependent benefits and can be less effective. Aggregate repair outcomes remain close to baseline, with token savings in selected settings. These findings support proactive runtime assistance for autonomous tool use. The gap between behavioral adjustment and aggregate repair gains calls for careful decisions on intervention timing and assistance strategy in autonomous agents.

papers.title: ARMOR: Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise-Robust RAG Reasoning
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. However, the retrieval process inevitably introduces noise, posing significant challenges to RAG robustness. Fundamentally, noise robustness is a composite competency encompassing noise identification, retrieval filtering, and robust reasoning. Unfortunately, existing methods often fail to capture this holistic nature, typically restricted to single-dimensional enhancements or hampered by noise-induced optimization interference. To address these limitations, we decompose RAG robustness into three sub-tasks: knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning. Accordingly, we propose ARMOR, an Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise Robust RAG Reasoning. Inspired by the teaching process, ARMOR introduces an adaptive task scheduler as a teacher to curate training plans according to the absolute learning progress of RAG generators (Student). Distinct from GRPO, ARMOR utilizes inter-group advantage estimation during learning to effectively mitigate mode collapse caused by limited output spaces. Experiments on three complex reasoning datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA) indicate that ARMOR achieves synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness, significantly outperforming baselines in output quality.

papers.title: guardscope: Measuring Which Actions Runtime Controls Check in LLM Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Large-language model (LLM) agents execute actions on external systems through tool calls, and enterprises deploy runtime controls, such as agent gateways, to check this behavior in real time. However, a control can only evaluate the actions that cross the point where it is placed, and an agent can act through more paths than the tool-call channel; no existing work measures this coverage against kernel-level ground truth. In this paper, we present guardscope, a framework that makes this coverage measurable. guardscope works in two stages: a static stage that predicts which of an agent's 15 action paths a control can check from its source, and an empirical stage that runs a fixed workload on a deployment that realizes one of eight topology designs and classifies every executed action as checked, bypassed, or prevented by reconciling the control's decision records against kernel-level ground truth. guardscope makes a control's coverage claim verifiable: a runtime control developer can publish which paths its product inspects under a kernel-verified protocol. We conducted experiments with two agent harnesses and real runtime controls, including Microsoft's agent governance toolkit and agentgateway. guardscope is available at https://github.com/VulcanLab/guardscope.

papers.title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

papers.title: Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents often fail to meet all requirements in the task description. In some of these failures, the agent considers an implementation choice that meets a requirement, but later decides to commit to another one that does not meet the requirement for a reason it finds acceptable. We call this specification satisficing. It is challenging to identify and mitigate specification satisficing because the agent accepts such choices for its own reasons, and existing self-correction methods are biased toward them. We propose SatisFix, which guides a coding agent to report these choices and their reasons, and then check each choice against the task description. We evaluate SatisFix on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Pro with five LLMs as backbones and two different agent frameworks, and compare it with three self-correction methods. SatisFix improves the pass@1 of the base agent by an average of 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro. On DeepSWE, it outperforms the best baseline by 3.98%. Our ablation study shows that both steps of SatisFix contribute to the improvement.

papers.title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. Current agents shrink this history by having a model summarize it, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history it replaces, and cache-aware triggers decide when to compact while taking the size of the result as given. We present Folio, a context manager that records, folds, and recovers history through one set of handles. While the agent runs, Folio records three linked levels: a short turn note the model writes as part of its ordinary reply (L1), an event manifest of every call written by the runtime (L2), and the captured source records (L3). Because these views already exist, the runtime folds the context programmatically, selecting coarser views for older turns. The fold prints the handles that index L2 and L3, so recovery tools that read bounded pages, compute over full text in files, and keep findings in a persistent dossier reach the evidence the agent needs with little added input. The fold trigger prices an explicit landing point that includes the retained budget. On 75 LOCA-bench tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Pro behind every system, Folio solves 66 tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction and 49-59 for Claude Code, Codex, and SoL-Pi, in about half their working time, at 2.4 times lower cost than that runtime; each fold takes a median of 0.6 seconds.

papers.title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

papers.title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.

papers.title: CoLFA: Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Failure attribution in multi-agent systems requires tracing error formation to identify the decisive error step and the responsible agent. However, agents' division of work and information exchange lead to Interleaved Steps and Cluttered Content, requiring models to link executions and check details in lengthy records. This makes it difficult to balance localization accuracy and token cost. We find that multi-agent collaboration also leaves records of how executions connect and content passes between them as results are formed, providing evidence for tracing error formation. Based on this observation, we propose CoLFA (Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution), which uses collaboration cues to organize the attribution input according to how results are formed, determining which steps are examined and how their content is presented. Through Handoff-Guided Step Expansion and Cross-Referenced Content Organization, CoLFA helps the model focus on examining error formation and the role of each decision while reducing the processing of irrelevant and repeated records. Across five settings spanning Who&When and LongRCA and three backbone models, CoLFA achieves the highest exact step-localization accuracy with the lowest token consumption. Compared with individual baselines in each setting, CoLFA improves accuracy by up to 37.50% and reduces token consumption by up to 97.6%.

papers.title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_α$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.

papers.title: Testing Conversation Preservation Across LLM APIs: A Rule-Based Oracle for Detecting Silent Information Loss
papers.abstract: LLM applications increasingly rely on translators and compatibility layers to move conversations across APIs. Yet a translated request can be accepted by the target API while silently losing information about instruction roles, tool interactions, error states, or generation controls. We introduce isloss, a deterministic oracle for testing conversation-information preservation across LLM API translations. It maps source and translated requests and replies to a shared intermediate representation, ConvIR, and applies explicit rules to distinguish legitimate representation changes from information loss. Unlike schema validation or reference-based differential testing, isloss requires neither a reference translation nor additional model calls. It also distinguishes avoidable loss from degradation caused by target API limitations. We evaluate isloss using specification-based fault injection, human review, and experiments on translators, gateways, and client libraries. On held-out tests, it detects 95/125 planted faults (76.0%) with 2/100 false alarms (2.0%). Across a synthetic request suite spanning six configurations of five translator codebases, 127/685 completed translations (18.5%) pass static target checks while silently changing prompt, role, or tool information in ways the target API could have preserved. In translated replies, 203/558 streams (36.4%) cause exceptions or silent corruption in at least one tested official OpenAI SDK. Targeted experiments across six models show that translation-induced changes can alter model behaviour when tasks depend on the affected information. These results establish conversation preservation as a distinct correctness requirement for reliable LLM interoperability, agent execution, and model evaluation.

papers.title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simultaneously: completing the user's task (utility) and conforming to domain policies and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension -- blocking an unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other. We introduce Soteria, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajectories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.

papers.title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems
papers.abstract: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams

papers.title: Planners Exploit Deterministic Error: Dithered Low-Bit World Models
papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.

papers.title: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs
papers.abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.

papers.title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
papers.abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.

papers.title: Precision on Demand: Escalating Weight Bits at Uncertain Decoding Steps in a Small Local Model
papers.abstract: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.

papers.title: SFU-Sim: Bit-Exact Reverse Engineering of NVIDIA MUFU and Validation of PTX Paths
papers.abstract: Reproducing the numerical behavior of a GPU requires predicting the exact output of special function instructions. Vendor documents give only the function semantics and error bounds. These do not fix the output bit pattern. We present SFU-Sim, which builds bit-exact models of NVIDIA multi-function unit (MUFU) instructions by black-box reverse engineering on real GPUs. We first model a single bare MUFU instruction. We then add the surrounding operations found in the disassembly to model full PTX paths. The model covers 12 common MUFU forms and two BF16 forms on the tested Blackwell GPU. Using SIN/COS as a complete case study, we show how we analyze the PTX-to-SASS compilation path and recover the segment structure, the equivalent coefficient tables, and the finite-width arithmetic. On NVIDIA GPUs of three architectures (Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Blackwell), we exhaustively compare every tested PTX path over its specified input domain. FP16 and FP32 paths cover all $2^{16}$ and $2^{32}$ input encodings, respectively. The model output matches the hardware bit for bit, with zero mismatches. SFU-Sim computes each output directly from its input. It needs neither a lookup table of all inputs nor access to a physical GPU. It can serve as a bit-exact special function component for instruction simulators. It can also serve as an arithmetic reference for hardware design and functional verification that target the same numerical behavior. SFU-Sim and its validation programs are open source at https://github.com/hzX40000000/SFU-Sim

papers.title: Gradient-Guided Hardware-Native MIXFP4
papers.abstract: Blackwell tensor cores support native inference with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), but NVFP4 leaves a perplexity (PPL) gap to BF16. Choosing a format for each 16-element block can improve accuracy, but current matrix multiply instructions cannot execute choices this fine. Applying these rules at hardware-compatible tiles loses most of their benefit. We introduce FlipQuant, which selects E2M1 or E0M3 for each MMA weight tile. It keeps both quantized weight candidates fixed and learns a binary format map from end-to-end gradients of a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher, re-evaluating them after each update. Native kernels execute 16 x 64 tiles on SM120 and 256 x 64 tiles on SM100 with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Across six language models and two corpora, FlipQuant at 16 x 64 closes 42.5% of NVFP4's PPL gap to BF16 on average, compared with 13.3% for FourOverSix. Code is available at https://github.com/brian030128/flipquant.

papers.title: Pairwise distortion distribution for compression and quantization
